statement: The Los Angeles Rams played an American football game against the Green Bay Packers in Week 1 of the 1982 National Football League (NFL) season on September 12, 1982, at Milwaukee County Stadium in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, United States.
The Rams had missed the playoffs in 1981 for the first time in eight seasons.
The Packers had not been to the playoffs since 1972.
The Packers had not won a playoff game since 1967.
The Rams began the game strong, scoring 23 points in the first half, while shutting the Packers out.
The Rams took advantage of five Packers' first half turnovers.
Quarterback Lynn Dickey led the Packers to 35 unanswered points off of five touchdown drives.
The Packers defense held the Rams to just four first downs in the second half, while intercepting the Rams twice and forcing a fumble.
The 23-point comeback was the largest by the Packers up to that point.
The 23-point comeback was later matched in 2013 in a game against the Dallas Cowboys.
The game has been mentioned multiple times as one of the best in the history of the Rams versus the Packers.
The Rams had been perennial contenders for most of the 1970s.
The Packers had not won a playoff game since 1967, under Vince Lombardi.
Bart Starr was brought in as head coach to try to revive the Packers' success of the 1960s.
Starr accumulated a record of 39–65–2 in his first seven seasons.
Starr's record was the worst record of any head coach in league history through their first seven seasons.
In 1981, the Packers went 8–8.
The Packers missed out on the playoffs in 1981 by losing the last game of the season to the New York Jets, 28–3.
Starr signed a contract extension in the offseason based on the team's strong finish.
The Packers had gone 6–2 in their last eight games in 1981.
Going into 1982, the Packers offense was led by Lynn Dickey, James Lofton, and John Jefferson.
After missing the playoffs in 1981, the Rams brought in veteran players.
The Rams signed quarterback Bert Jones and tight end Mike Barber.
The game was played in Milwaukee instead of Green Bay due to scheduling conflicts later in the year with the Milwaukee Brewers.
The Rams took advantage of three Packers' turnovers to take a commanding lead into halftime.
In the first quarter, Gerry Ellis fumbled the ball on a short run.
The fumbled ball was returned by the Rams to mid-field.
A 22-yard pass from Jones to Wendell Tyler moved the Rams close.
Wendell Tyler took a short rush into the end zone to put the Rams up 7–0.
Another Packers fumble occurred, this time by Dickey while he was avoiding the Rams' pass rush.
An offensive penalty forced the Rams to accept a short field goal attempt.
Mike Lansford converted the field goal attempt to increase the lead to 10–0.
After a 43-yard pass from Jones to Willie Miller put the Rams in scoring position, Jones completed an eight-yard pass to Barber for a touchdown, bringing the score to 17–0.
The Rams had two more scoring drives.
Each of the Rams' two additional scoring drives ended in a Lansford field goal.
The first additional field goal was set-up by a long punt return.
The second additional field goal came after Dickey threw an interception to Carl Ekern.
The Rams took a 23–0 lead into halftime.
The Packers scored 35 unanswered points in the second half.
The Packers had their first score on a short touchdown pass from Dickey to Paul Coffman.
The Packers moved into scoring position after a defensive pass interference penalty gave the Packers 28 yards.
The Packers struck again, this time on a short run from Eddie Lee Ivery for a touchdown.
The key play of the drive was a 42-yard pass completion from Dickey to Coffman.
By the end of the third quarter, the Packers had cut the Rams lead to 23–14.
At the beginning of the fourth quarter, the Rams were stopped by the Packers defense.
Mike Lansford missed a long field goal attempt.
On the ensuing drive, Dickey completed a 50-yard pass to Jefferson.
Dickey threw his second touchdown pass, a 15-yard completion to Lofton, a few plays later.
With the score now 23–21, the Packers kicked off to the Rams.
On the kick-off return, Robert Alexander fumbled the ball.
The Packers recovered the fumbled ball at the 10-yard line.
On the next play, Dickey threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Coffman to give the Packers their first lead, 28–23.
The Packers sealed their comeback victory with a 27-yard rushing touchdown by Ivery with about three minutes left in the game.
The Packers won 35–23.
The game was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
The game time was 1:00 p.m. CST.
The weather was 73°F, with wind.
The attendance was 53,694.
The game was televised by CBS.
The announcers were Jack Buck and Hank Stram.

On September 21, 1982, the NFL Players Association went on strike.
The strike originated from the players demanding a greater share of revenue.
The players settled for modest increases in salary and benefits.
As a result of the strike, the season was shortened to nine games.
The playoffs were expanded to the top eight teams from each conference, regardless of division.
The Packers ended the season 5–3–1.
The Packers made the playoffs for the first time since 1972.
The Rams went 2–7.
The Rams missed out on a playoff berth.
The Packers beat the St. Louis Cardinals 41–16 in the first round of the playoffs.
The Packers' victory against the St. Louis Cardinals was their first postseason victory since 1967.
The Packers lost in the second round of the playoffs to the Dallas Cowboys by a score of 37–26.
The Rams fired head coach Ray Malavasi at the end of the season.
The game marked the largest comeback in Packers' history at the time.
The previous largest comeback was an 18-point comeback during a 1965 regular season game against the Lions.
The 23-point comeback mark was matched 31 years later.
The Packers beat the Dallas Cowboys during a 2013 regular season game after falling behind by 23 points.
Multiple post-game articles referenced the Packers matching their comeback record from the Rams game.
In a 2004 article, former Packers' team historian Lee Remmel identified the comeback as a key moment in the Packers history against the Rams.
Two years later, Remmel provided an in-depth overview of the comeback as part of his historical coverage in preparation for a Packers game against the Rams.
In describing the game, Remmel noted the drastic change at halftime, with the Packers defense shutting the Rams out, while Dickey and the Packers offense exploded for five touchdowns.
In his book chronicling the first 100 years of Packers history, Cliff Christl described the comeback against the Rams as 'an inspiring and record-setting comeback'.
Christl highlighted the contributions of Dickey, Coffman, Jefferson, and Lofton.

In his book Green Bay Packers: Trials, Triumphs, and Tradition, author William Povletich noted that the Packers 'displayed their firepower with a spirited second-half comeback' because 'their offense had found its stride, becoming as explosive as any in football'.
Povletich also discussed the atmosphere the game was played in revolving around the possibility of a player strike.
Multiple football bloggers have also written extensively about the game.
